content.text:
## Factual research brief

### 1. `tlsVersion` passed to `SSLContext.getInstance(...)`

| Expression | Declaring type identifiable from supplied imports | Exact runtime string value(s) |
|---|---|---|
| `tlsVersion` | **Not identifiable.** None of the supplied imports declares a symbol named `tlsVersion`; they import `SSLContext`, `SSLSocketFactory`, `TrustManager`, `X509TrustManager`, and exception classes only. The declaration could be a local parameter/variable, property, or member of an unprovided type. | **Unresolved.** The supplied material does not include its declaration, initializer, or call arguments, so no exact value can be established. |

`SSLContext.getInstance` takes a Java `String` protocol argument. Thus, for the Kotlin call to type-check, `tlsVersion` must be compatible with Java `String`; that establishes only the argument type, **not** its declaring owner or its runtime contents. Oracle specifies that the argument is the standard name of the requested secure-socket protocol. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html?utm_source=openai))

The Java Security Standard Algorithm Names specification defines standard `SSLContext` names including `TLS`, `TLSv1`, `TLSv1.1`, `TLSv1.2`, `TLSv1.3`, `DTLS`, `DTLSv1.0`, and `DTLSv1.2`. This list is **not evidence** that `tlsVersion` evaluates to any particular member of it; a provider may also recognize provider-specific names or aliases. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html?utm_source=openai))

### 2. Applicable standard/API semantics

The finding’s `SSLContextSpec` and `UnsatisfiedConstraint` labels do not, from the supplied metadata, identify a published TLS/WebDAV/IETF interoperability requirement that fixes an exact `tlsVersion` literal. The relevant published interface contract is the Java JSSE `SSLContext` API and Java Security Standard Algorithm Names specification—not an RFC that mandates a Java `getInstance(...)` argument string.

For `SSLContext.getInstance(String)`:

- The value selects a provider implementation for a requested secure-socket protocol; it does **not** by itself establish which protocol versions are enabled on sockets/engines or which version is ultimately negotiated. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html?utm_source=openai))
- Oracle documents that a context obtained with, for example, `getInstance("TLSv1")` may implement TLS 1.0, 1.1, and 1.2; enabled protocols are controlled separately on the created TLS endpoint. Therefore, no conclusion about legacy-protocol enablement or negotiated version follows from an unknown `tlsVersion` value alone. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html?utm_source=openai))
- The standardized name `TLS` is an extensible/provider-selected request meaning “supports some version of TLS” and may support other SSL/TLS versions. It is not a fixed wire-protocol pin. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html?utm_source=openai))

For the detector message concerning `TrustManager[]` passed to `SSLContext.init(...)`:

- Java defines the `tm` argument as sources of peer-authentication trust decisions. If it is `null`, the installed providers are searched for an appropriate trust-manager-factory implementation; where a non-null array is supplied, only the first manager of a particular implementation type is used. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html?utm_source=openai))
- Java’s `TrustManager` contract expressly allows managers to be created either by a `TrustManagerFactory` **or by implementing a TrustManager subtype**. Thus, the detector’s provenance condition—requiring an observed factory origin—is not itself a Java SE API requirement. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManager.html?utm_source=openai))
- For X.509 server authentication, `X509TrustManager.checkServerTrusted` is specified to build a path to a trusted root and return only when the chain is validated and trusted; it throws `CertificateException` when the chain is not trusted. The supplied finding does not establish whether the application-defined manager satisfies these semantics. ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/X509TrustManager.html?utm_source=openai))

### Source limitations and externally unresolved questions

```text
externally_unresolved_questions:
- What declaration owns tlsVersion, and what initializer or call-site values can reach it?
- Which Java/Android runtime and JSSE provider version supplies SSLContext?
- Are protocols separately enabled or constrained after the SSLSocketFactory is obtained?
- Does the supplied TrustManager preserve X.509 chain-validation semantics, and is endpoint identity verification configured at the relevant connection layer?
- The detector message alone does not identify a WebDAV-server requirement, a TLS RFC version requirement, or a mandated literal value for tlsVersion.
```

This pass did not inspect the repository or infer the behavior of the reported method; therefore it cannot resolve the runtime string or evaluate the supplied trust-manager implementation.

### Official sources

- Oracle Java `SSLContext` API: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/26/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/SSLContext.html?utm_source=openai))
- Oracle Java Security Standard Algorithm Names: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/specs/security/standard-names.html?utm_source=openai))
- Oracle JSSE Reference Guide: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/25/security/java-secure-socket-extension-jsse-reference-guide.html?utm_source=openai))
- Oracle Java `TrustManager` API: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManager.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/TrustManager.html?utm_source=openai))
- Oracle Java `X509TrustManager` API: https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/X509TrustManager.html ([docs.oracle.com](https://docs.oracle.com/en/java/javase/17/docs/api/java.base/javax/net/ssl/X509TrustManager.html?utm_source=openai))
